opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, GEAR — the Generalist Embodied Agent Research group — is ultimately about building foundation models for agents that act, not just models that talk or generate pixels. And we take "embodied" in a broad sense: an agent can be embodied in a physical robot, but it can also be embodied in a virtual world, like a game or a simulation. To me those are two sides of the same coin.

The big picture is what I sometimes call the "foundation agent" idea. We've seen language models become generalists across text tasks. The next frontier is a single model, or a family of models, that can generalize across many different bodies and many different realities. Today a robot policy is usually trained for one specific robot doing one specific task. We want to move away from that toward something that learns skills that transfer, whether it's a humanoid in a factory, a robot arm in a kitchen, or a character in Minecraft.

Why virtual and physical together? Because the physical world is expensive and slow. You can't parallelize real-world robot data collection the way you can with internet text. So simulation becomes really important. In simulation you can run thousands of environments in parallel, at many times real-time speed, with randomized physics and visuals, and then try to transfer what was learned into the real world. Games and open-ended virtual worlds are also wonderful testbeds for things like long-horizon planning, curiosity, and lifelong learning. That's where some of our earlier work, like MineDojo and Voyager, came from.

On the physical side, a lot of our focus now is on humanoid robots — Project GR00T is the flagship there — because the world is built around the human form, and humanoids can in principle leverage human data and human environments directly.

So the mission, in one sentence: build generalist agents that learn across many simulated and real worlds, and eventually make "physical AI" as capable and general as what we've seen from language models. I think of it as solving the data problem and the generalization problem for robotics at the same time, and simulation plus internet-scale data plus real robot data is the recipe we're betting on.

r001.rationale: The candidate says GEAR builds foundation models for agents that act and treats physical and virtual embodiment as two sides of the same coin, framing action as their shared task.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about GEAR is that the name is really the mission statement. Generalist, embodied, agent, research. Each word is load-bearing.

"Generalist" is the key one. Historically, robotics and game AI were built one task at a time. You'd train a policy to stack blocks, and that policy knew nothing about opening a drawer. We want the opposite: one foundation model that can take in multimodal input, whether that's pixels, language, proprioception, and output actions across a huge range of tasks and embodiments. The same way GPT isn't a "summarization model" or a "translation model," we don't want a "pick-and-place model." We want a brain.

"Embodied" means the model doesn't just talk about the world, it acts in it. And that's where the virtual-versus-physical split comes in, which honestly I see less as a split and more as a continuum. On the virtual side, we've done things like Voyager in Minecraft, where an agent writes its own skill library and keeps exploring without a human defining the curriculum. On the physical side, we have humanoids, where the goal is to go from videos and simulation to a robot that can actually do useful work in a kitchen or a warehouse.

The reason we do both under one roof is data. Language models got to eat the entire internet. Robots don't have an internet of actions. So we have to manufacture that data, and simulation is the engine. We can run thousands of GPU-accelerated environments in parallel, randomize physics and visuals, and generate years of experience in hours. Virtual worlds are also where we can be ambitious about open-endedness, because failure is free there. Then the hard, humbling part is closing the sim-to-real gap and having those skills survive contact with the real world.

So if I compress it into one sentence: we're trying to build the foundation model for agents that act, and we treat games, simulators, and physical robots as different bodies for the same mind. The long-term bet is that one day the distinction between "this agent plays Minecraft" and "this agent folds your laundry" will feel as outdated as "this model does sentiment analysis."

r001.rationale: The response describes a shared foundation model that outputs actions across many tasks and embodiments, and treats games, simulators, and physical robots as different bodies for the same mind.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about our mission is to build generalist agents that can perceive, reason, and act across many different environments. That includes physical robots, but also agents in simulated worlds and video games. The common thread is an agent that learns through interaction, rather than only learning to predict text.

Today, we often build a specialized system for a particular robot or a particular task. We want to move toward a shared foundation: a model that can transfer what it learns across tasks, environments, and even different kinds of bodies.

Virtual worlds are important because they give us a place to scale experience. You can expose an agent to diverse situations, let it make mistakes, and learn without the cost and constraints of physical hardware. But simulation is a means, not the end. The challenge is turning that experience into useful behavior in the real world. So we see virtual and physical intelligence as connected parts of the same research agenda.

r001.rationale: The response says agents should perceive, reason, and act across environments, but identifies learning through interaction—not action generation—as the common thread unifying the work.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about our mission is to build generalist agents that can perceive, reason, and act across both virtual and physical worlds. That could mean a character in a video game or a robot operating in the real world. The environments are different, but the core question is similar: how do you build an agent that can learn many skills and adapt to new situations, rather than being engineered for one narrow task?

Virtual worlds are especially useful because they let us scale experience. We can run many environments in parallel, vary the conditions, and let agents practice things that would be slow or difficult to collect on physical hardware. The challenge is turning that experience into capabilities that transfer.

Ultimately, we want to move from specialists toward a shared foundation for embodied intelligence—agents that can take a goal, understand their surroundings, and figure out how to act.

r001.rationale: It describes agents that perceive, reason, and act in both virtual and physical worlds, and says the shared goal is to understand surroundings and figure out how to act.
